extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing patent eligibility under Alice/Mayo, including considerations for improvements to technology, particular machines, particular transformations, and whether additional elements are well‑understood, routine, and conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to existing technology consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of improvements is relevant to the eligibility analysis regardless of the technology of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The invention may be eligible if the claim describes an improvement to technology (e.g., improved way of preserving cells or improved computer animation) rather than merely reciting an idea or outcome. An improvement in the abstract idea itself (e.g., a recited fundamental economic concept) is not an improvement in technology. See McRO and Rapid Litigation Management examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of improvements that may show an improvement in technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Court-indicated examples that may be sufficient to show an improvement in existing technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes particular computerized method of operating a rubber molding press (Diamond v. Diehr), new telephone/server combinations (TLI Communications), advances in downloading for streaming (Affinity Labs), improved digital data compression (DDR Holdings, Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec), particular virus-screening methods for the Internet (Symantec), measurement devices/techniques that generate new data (Electric Power Group v. Alstom), particular configurations of inertial sensors and methods of using raw sensor data (Thales Visionix), specific structured GUIs that improve transaction accuracy (Trading Techs. v. CQG), and improved processes for preserving hepatocytes (Rapid Litig. Mgmt.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples that may not show an improvement to technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Court-indicated examples that may be insufficient to show an improvement to technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes applying commonplace business methods on a general purpose computer (Alice, Versata), using well-known lab techniques to detect enzyme levels (Cleveland Clinic), gathering/analyzing information with conventional techniques and displaying results (TLI), delivering broadcast content at a high level of generality (Affinity Labs cases), general email screening on a generic computer (Symantec), mere advances in informational content of a download for streaming, and selecting a type of content or generic hardware function from within a range of existing options (Affinity Labs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must recite how a computer aids the method (not generic computer addition)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that involvement of a computer assists in improving the technology, the claims must recite the details regarding how a computer aids the method, the extent to which the computer aids the method, or the significance of a computer to the performance of the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely adding generic computer components or generic instructions to perform the method on conventional machinery is not sufficient. If applicant adds a generic computer or claims a 'specially programmed' computer, the examiner must assess whether the added elements integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more than the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test as investigatory clue (not stand-alone)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The machine-or-transformation test is a useful and important clue, and investigative tool" for determining patent eligibility, but it is not a stand‑alone test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All claims must be evaluated under the Alice/Mayo two-part test. A claim that passes Alice/Mayo is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test; conversely a claim that fails Alice/Mayo is ineligible even if it passes the M-or-T test. Use M-or-T along with other considerations (mere instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of machine/apparatus elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the degree to which the machine in the claim can be specifically identified (not any and all machines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A particular machine recited with specific structural details (e.g., types/arrangement/shape of components) supports integration of the exception into a practical application. General purpose computers that apply an exception via conventional functions do not qualify as a particular machine. See Mackay Radio, Eibel Process, and Ultramercial/TLI/Eon examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the machine/apparatus implements the method steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the machine plays an integral role in performing the claimed method steps rather than merely being an object on which the method operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integral use of a machine to achieve performance of a method can integrate the judicial exception into a practical application; mere use of a machine as a tool to perform an existing process (or obvious speed-up) will generally not amount to significantly more. See CyberSource and Versata discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the machine's involvement is extra-solution activity or field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the extent to which the machine or apparatus imposes meaningful limits on the claim versus contributing only nominally to execution of the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use that contributes only nominally (e.g., data-gathering or identifying a data source) or field-of-use limitations generally do not integrate a judicial exception or provide significantly more. See Bilski, Parker v. Flook, and CyberSource examples; see MPEP §§2106.05(g) & (h) for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation consideration (transformation/reduction of an article)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing is a clue to patentability of a process that does not include particular machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation of a particular article to a different state or thing may indicate the claim is significantly more or integrates the exception into a practical application. This is a useful clue but not a stand-alone test; evaluate alongside Alice/Mayo and other considerations. An 'article' includes a physical object or substance; pure mental processes are not eligible transformations. For data, mere manipulation of mathematical constructs is not considered a transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation factor: particularity or generality of the transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how definite or particular the transformation is (e.g., chemical/physical processes that confine the monopoly to definite bounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More particular transformations (tanning, dyeing, vulcanizing, smelting examples) are more likely to provide significantly more. See Gottschalk v. Benson discussion of Corning v. Burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation factor: degree to which the recited article is particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the transformation applies to a specifically identified article or to generically recited articles (any and all articles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation applied to a generically recited article or to any and all articles is less likely to provide significantly more; a transformation limited to particular articles is more likely to provide significantly more or integrate the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation factor: nature and extent of change in state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the type/extent of change effected by the claimed transformation (different function/use vs. mere location change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformations that result in the article having a different function or use are more likely to provide significantly more; mere relocation or insignificant change is less likely. Example: transforming uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded products (Diehr) provides significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation factor: nature of the article transformed
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the transformed article is physical/tangible or an intangible concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation of a physical or tangible object/substance is more likely to provide significantly more than transformation of an intangible concept (e.g., contractual obligation or mental judgment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation factor: whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the recited transformation merely imposes a field-of-use limitation or contributes only nominally to execution of the claimed method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation that is merely a field-of-use limitation or contributes only nominally (e.g., data gathering or routine administration steps) likely will not provide significantly more. Example: Supreme Court in Mayo found administering a drug was only a field-of-use limitation and did not supply significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2B, consider whether additional element(s) are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements are merely well-understood, routine, conventional activities recited at a high level of generality, they do not favor eligibility. If the additional elements are specific limitations that are unconventional or confine the claim to a particular useful application, they favor eligibility. Examples: DDR Holdings (favored eligibility) vs. Mayo (did not favor). This consideration overlaps with improvement, mere instructions, and insignificant extra-solution activity considerations (see MPEP §§2106.05(a),(f),(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Known-in-the-art elements can still be non-routine/unconventional
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element (or combination of additional elements) that is known in the art can nevertheless be unconventional or non-routine for eligibility purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability (novelty/obviousness) is distinct from eligibility. Features taught by prior art may still be considered unconventional in the eligibility analysis if they represent an improvement to conventional functionality (example: Enfish). Examiners should evaluate whether the claimed features are 'conventional' in the context of eligibility even if they are not novel.
